title: Python for QA Testers
description: A complete Python foundation for QA engineers — language fundamentals, pytest mastery, API testing, UI automation bindings, and CI/CD, built for testers who want real engineering depth, not just scripts.

lessons.title: Why Python for QA
lessons.description: Understand the ecosystem that makes Python the default QA language in 2026.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The QA Python Ecosystem

Python dominates test automation not because of the language alone, but because of the ecosystem built around it:

- **pytest** — the de facto test runner, with the richest fixture/plugin ecosystem of any language
- **requests** / **httpx** — the standard for API testing
- **Selenium** and **Playwright** Python bindings — full parity with their JS counterparts
- **pydantic** — schema validation for API contract testing
- **Allure** / **pytest-html** — professional-grade reporting

This course builds each of these skills in order: language fundamentals first, then pytest, then API testing, then UI automation — so by the capstone you're combining all of them into one real suite, not learning them as disconnected tricks.
lessons.starter_code:
# Python's role in QA: readable syntax + a mature testing ecosystem
# (pytest, requests, Selenium/Playwright bindings) built on top of it.
print("Let's build real QA engineering skills.")

lessons.title: Variables, Data Types & Control Flow for Test Scripts
lessons.description: The Python fundamentals you'll use in every single test you write.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Building Blocks

```python
# Variables & core types
base_url = "https://api.example.com"
max_retries = 3
timeout_seconds = 10.5
is_authenticated = False

# Lists and dicts — you'll use these constantly for test data
user_roles = ["admin", "editor", "viewer"]
expected_response = {"status": "ok", "code": 200}

# Control flow
for role in user_roles:
    if role == "admin":
        print(f"Testing admin-only endpoints for role: {role}")
    else:
        print(f"Testing standard access for role: {role}")

# List comprehensions — concise, common in real test code
active_users = [u for u in get_users() if u["status"] == "active"]
```

If you're coming from another language, Python's biggest adjustment is significant whitespace (indentation defines blocks, not braces) and duck typing (variables aren't declared with a fixed type). Both make test scripts faster to write once they're second nature.

quiz_data.question: In Python, what defines the boundaries of a code block (like an if statement's body)?
options: Curly braces { }
Indentation (whitespace)
The 'end' keyword
Semicolons
quiz_data.explanation: Python uses significant whitespace/indentation to define blocks instead of braces or keywords — a key adjustment for developers coming from C-style languages.

lessons.title: Functions, Modules & Virtual Environments
lessons.description: Organize test code properly from day one.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Functions

```python
def build_test_user(role="student", verified=True):
    return {"email": f"test-{role}@example.com", "role": role, "verified": verified}

admin_user = build_test_user(role="admin")
```

## Modules

Split test helpers into importable files instead of one giant script:
```python
# helpers/users.py
def build_test_user(role="student"):
    ...

# test_signup.py
from helpers.users import build_test_user
```

## Virtual Environments — Non-Negotiable

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pytest requests selenium
pip freeze > requirements.txt
```

A virtual environment isolates your project's dependencies from your system Python and from other projects. Skipping this is the #1 cause of "it works on my machine but not in CI" for Python test suites — different projects silently depending on conflicting library versions installed globally.

lessons.title: Working with Files & JSON
lessons.description: Manage test fixtures and data the way real suites do.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Reading Test Data from JSON

```python
import json

with open("fixtures/users.json") as f:
    test_users = json.load(f)

for user in test_users:
    print(user["email"], user["role"])
```

## Writing Results

```python
results = {"passed": 42, "failed": 1, "skipped": 3}
with open("results/summary.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(results, f, indent=2)
```

Keeping test data in JSON fixture files (rather than hardcoded in test functions) means non-engineers can update test data, and the same fixture can be reused across many tests without duplication.

lessons.title: Pytest Basics: Discovery, Assertions & Fixtures
lessons.description: Understand how pytest actually finds and runs your tests.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Test Discovery

Pytest automatically finds tests using naming conventions: files named `test_*.py` or `*_test.py`, functions named `test_*`, classes named `Test*`.

```python
# test_math.py
def test_addition():
    assert 2 + 2 == 4

def test_string_formatting():
    name = "Zaka"
    assert f"Hello, {name}" == "Hello, Zaka"
```

## Plain `assert` — No Special Syntax Needed

Unlike many frameworks, pytest uses Python's built-in `assert` and rewrites it to give rich failure output automatically:
```
>       assert 2 + 2 == 5
E       assert 4 == 5
```

## Fixtures: Reusable Setup

```python
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def api_client():
    client = ApiClient(base_url="https://api.example.com")
    yield client
    client.close()  # teardown runs after the test

def test_get_users(api_client):
    response = api_client.get("/users")
    assert response.status_code == 200
```

The `yield` splits a fixture into setup (before) and teardown (after) — pytest guarantees the teardown runs even if the test fails.

quiz_data.question: In a pytest fixture using yield, what happens to the code after the yield statement?
options: It never runs
It runs as teardown after the test completes, even if the test fails
It runs before the test as additional setup
It only runs if the test passes
quiz_data.explanation: yield splits a fixture into setup (before yield) and teardown (after yield). Pytest guarantees the teardown code runs regardless of whether the test passed or failed.

lessons.title: Parametrization & Data-Driven Tests
lessons.description: Run one test function against many inputs cleanly.
lessons.content_markdown:
## `@pytest.mark.parametrize`

```python
import pytest

@pytest.mark.parametrize("email,is_valid", [
    ("user@example.com", True),
    ("not-an-email", False),
    ("", False),
    ("user@sub.example.com", True),
])
def test_email_validation(email, is_valid):
    assert validate_email(email) == is_valid
```

Running `pytest -v` shows each case as its own labeled result:
```
test_email_validation[user@example.com-True] PASSED
test_email_validation[not-an-email-False] PASSED
```

This is the single highest-leverage pytest feature for QA work — most real-world test coverage gaps come from under-testing input variations, and parametrization makes covering them nearly free.

lessons.title: Fixture Scopes & conftest.py
lessons.description: Share setup efficiently across many test files.
lessons.content_markdown:
## `conftest.py`: Shared Fixtures Without Imports

Any fixture defined in `conftest.py` is automatically available to every test in that directory (and subdirectories) — no import needed.

```python
# conftest.py
import pytest

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def db_connection():
    conn = connect_to_test_db()
    yield conn
    conn.close()

@pytest.fixture(scope="function")
def clean_user_table(db_connection):
    db_connection.execute("DELETE FROM users")
    yield
```

## Scopes

- `function` (default) — runs once per test
- `class` — once per test class
- `module` — once per file
- `session` — once for the entire test run

Use `session` scope for expensive setup you truly only need once (a database connection); use `function` scope for anything that must be fresh per test (avoiding state leaking between tests, a classic source of order-dependent flakiness).

quiz_data.question: Why would you use scope='function' instead of scope='session' for a fixture that resets database state?
options: function scope is faster to type
Session scope only allows read operations
Function-scoped fixtures run fresh for every test, preventing state from one test leaking into another
There is no real difference between the two
quiz_data.explanation: A session-scoped reset would only run once for the whole test run, letting state accumulate across tests and causing order-dependent failures. Function scope guarantees a clean slate per test.

lessons.title: Markers, Skipping & Custom Configuration
lessons.description: Control exactly which tests run, and when.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Built-in Markers

```python
import pytest

@pytest.mark.skip(reason="Feature not deployed to staging yet")
def test_new_checkout_flow():
    ...

@pytest.mark.skipif(sys.platform == "win32", reason="POSIX-only file permissions test")
def test_file_permissions():
    ...

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="Known bug JIRA-4521")
def test_known_broken_feature():
    ...
```

## Custom Markers

```python
# pytest.ini
[pytest]
markers =
    smoke: quick sanity checks run on every commit
    regression: full suite run nightly
```
```bash
pytest -m smoke   # run only smoke-marked tests
```

Custom markers let a large suite be sliced by purpose — a fast "smoke" subset gates every commit, while the full "regression" suite runs on a schedule, without maintaining two separate test directories.

lessons.title: HTTP Fundamentals & the requests Library
lessons.description: Test REST APIs directly, without a browser.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Your First API Test

```python
import requests

def test_get_user():
    response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = response.json()
    assert data["id"] == 1
    assert "email" in data
```

## All the HTTP Verbs

```python
requests.get(url)
requests.post(url, json={"name": "New Course"})
requests.put(url, json={"name": "Updated Course"})
requests.patch(url, json={"price": 49.99})
requests.delete(url)
```

API tests run dramatically faster than UI tests (no browser startup, no rendering, no waits for animations) — this is why a well-designed test suite pushes as much coverage as possible down to the API layer, reserving UI tests for things that can only be verified visually.
lessons.starter_code:
import requests

def test_get_user():
    response = requests.get("https://api.example.com/users/1")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    data = response.json()
    assert data["id"] == 1

quiz_data.question: Why do well-designed test suites push as much coverage as possible into API tests rather than UI tests?
options: API tests are always more important to stakeholders
API tests run much faster since there's no browser startup, rendering, or animation waits involved
UI tests are being deprecated industry-wide
API tests don't require assertions
quiz_data.explanation: Without browser overhead, API tests execute in milliseconds instead of seconds, letting a suite run far more coverage in the same CI time budget — UI tests are reserved for what can only be verified visually.

lessons.title: Testing REST APIs: Status Codes, Headers & Schemas
lessons.description: Go beyond '200 OK' to real contract validation.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Thorough API Assertions

```python
def test_create_course():
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.example.com/courses",
        json={"title": "New Course", "price": 49.99},
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
    )

    assert response.status_code == 201
    assert response.headers["Content-Type"] == "application/json"

    data = response.json()
    assert data["title"] == "New Course"
    assert isinstance(data["id"], str)
    assert data["price"] == 49.99
```

## Schema Validation with `jsonschema`

```python
from jsonschema import validate

course_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["id", "title", "price"],
    "properties": {
        "id": {"type": "string"},
        "title": {"type": "string"},
        "price": {"type": "number"},
    },
}
validate(instance=response.json(), schema=course_schema)
```

Schema validation catches an entire category of bugs (a field silently becoming null, a type changing from number to string) that a handful of manual `assert` statements would easily miss.

lessons.title: Authentication Flows in API Tests
lessons.description: Handle the auth patterns you'll meet in almost every real API.

quiz_data.question: Why should an auth token be fetched in a session-scoped fixture rather than re-authenticated in every test?
options: Session scope is required by the requests library
Re-authenticating per test wastes time and can trigger rate limits on the auth endpoint
Tokens expire after one use
Function-scoped fixtures cannot make HTTP requests
quiz_data.explanation: Authenticating once per test session and reusing the token avoids unnecessary load on the auth endpoint and speeds up the overall suite significantly.

lessons.title: Selenium & Playwright Python Bindings
lessons.description: Compare the two major UI automation options available in Python.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Two Solid Choices

```python
# Selenium
from selenium import webdriver
driver = webdriver.Chrome()
driver.get("https://example.com")

# Playwright (sync API)
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
with sync_playwright() as p:
    browser = p.chromium.launch()
    page = browser.new_page()
    page.goto("https://example.com")
```

### When to choose which
- **Selenium**: broader industry adoption, W3C standard, best choice if your team already has Selenium infrastructure or needs Grid/cloud-provider compatibility
- **Playwright**: built-in auto-waiting, faster execution, better debugging tools (trace viewer) — the stronger choice for a brand-new project

Both are legitimate, widely-used choices in 2026 — this course covers Selenium bindings since they pair naturally with everything you've learned so far, but the concepts (locators, waits, page objects) transfer directly to Playwright's Python API too.
lessons.starter_code:
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.common.by import By

driver = webdriver.Chrome()
driver.get("https://example.com")
assert driver.find_element(By.TAG_NAME, "h1").text == "Example Domain"
driver.quit()

lessons.title: Combining Pytest + Selenium Cleanly
lessons.description: Wire up driver lifecycle management the right way.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Driver Fixture Pattern

```python
# conftest.py
import pytest
from selenium import webdriver

@pytest.fixture
def driver():
    options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument("--headless=new")
    drv = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
    drv.implicitly_wait(0)  # explicit waits only, as covered earlier
    yield drv
    drv.quit()
```

Every test that needs a browser just declares `driver` as a parameter — pytest handles creation and teardown automatically, and each test gets a **fresh browser instance**, eliminating state leakage between UI tests (cookies, localStorage, open tabs from a previous test).

```python
def test_login_page_loads(driver):
    driver.get("https://app.example.com/login")
    assert "Log In" in driver.title
```
lessons.starter_code:
import pytest
from selenium import webdriver

@pytest.fixture
def driver():
    options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
    options.add_argument("--headless=new")
    drv = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
    yield drv
    drv.quit()

def test_login_page_loads(driver):
    driver.get("https://app.example.com/login")
    assert "Log In" in driver.title

quiz_data.question: Why does putting the WebDriver instance in a pytest fixture help avoid flaky UI tests?
options: It makes tests run in parallel automatically
Each test gets a fresh browser instance, eliminating cookie/localStorage/tab state leaking between tests
Fixtures are required by Selenium
It removes the need for explicit waits
quiz_data.explanation: A function-scoped driver fixture creates a brand-new browser session per test and tears it down afterward, so no state (cookies, open tabs, storage) can leak from one test into the next.

lessons.title: Mocking External Services
lessons.description: Test code that depends on external APIs without calling them for real.
lessons.content_markdown:
## `unittest.mock`

```python
from unittest.mock import patch

def test_send_welcome_email(mocker):
    with patch("myapp.email.send") as mock_send:
        register_user("qa@zaka.dev")
        mock_send.assert_called_once_with(
            to="qa@zaka.dev", template="welcome"
        )
```

## Mocking HTTP with `responses`

```python
import responses

@responses.activate
def test_weather_lookup():
    responses.add(
        responses.GET, "https://api.weather.com/current",
        json={"temp": 72, "condition": "sunny"}, status=200
    )
    result = get_current_weather("San Francisco")
    assert result["temp"] == 72
```

Mocking lets you test your code's behavior in response to a *specific* external condition (a timeout, a 500 error, a malformed payload) without needing the real service to actually be in that state — often impossible or impractical to trigger for real.

quiz_data.question: What is the main advantage of mocking an external API's error response instead of trying to trigger a real error?
options: Mocking is required by pytest
It lets you deterministically test how your code handles a specific condition (timeout, 500 error) that would be impractical to trigger for real
It makes the real API faster
It removes the need for assertions
quiz_data.explanation: Real external services rarely let you reliably trigger a specific failure mode on demand; mocking makes edge-case testing deterministic and fast.

lessons.title: Test Data Management & Factories
lessons.description: Stop hand-writing repetitive test data dictionaries.
lessons.content_markdown:
## The Problem with Hardcoded Fixtures

```python
# Repetitive and brittle — every test redefines similar data
def test_a():
    user = {"email": "a@test.com", "role": "student", "plan": "free"}

def test_b():
    user = {"email": "b@test.com", "role": "student", "plan": "free"}
```

## `factory_boy`

```python
import factory

class UserFactory(factory.Factory):
    class Meta:
        model = dict

    email = factory.Sequence(lambda n: f"user{n}@test.com")
    role = "student"
    plan = "free"

# Usage
default_user = UserFactory()
admin_user = UserFactory(role="admin")
batch_of_users = UserFactory.create_batch(10)
```

Factories give you sensible defaults for every field, with the ability to override only what a specific test actually cares about — dramatically reducing test data boilerplate as a suite grows past a handful of tests.
lessons.starter_code:
import factory

class UserFactory(factory.Factory):
    class Meta:
        model = dict

    email = factory.Sequence(lambda n: f"user{n}@test.com")
    role = "student"
    plan = "free"

admin_user = UserFactory(role="admin")
print(admin_user)

lessons.title: Writing Maintainable, Readable Test Code
lessons.description: The style conventions that separate professional test code from scripts.
lessons.content_markdown:
## What Separates a Script from a Test Suite

- **PEP 8** — consistent formatting (use `black` or `ruff format` to enforce it automatically, don't debate it manually)
- **Type hints** — even in test code, they catch mistakes early and document intent
- **One assertion concept per test** — a test named `test_login` that also silently checks profile data, navigation, and analytics events is really three tests wearing one name
- **Descriptive test names** — `test_login_fails_with_wrong_password`, not `test_login_2`

```python
def build_test_user(role: str = "student", verified: bool = True) -> dict[str, str | bool]:
    return {"email": f"test-{role}@example.com", "role": role, "verified": verified}
```

Test code is production code — it will be read, debugged, and modified far more often than it's written. Treating it as disposable is exactly how a suite becomes unmaintainable within a year.
lessons.starter_code:
def build_test_user(role: str = "student", verified: bool = True) -> dict:
    return {"email": f"test-{role}@example.com", "role": role, "verified": verified}

lessons.title: Running Pytest in GitHub Actions
lessons.description: Wire your suite into a real automated pipeline.
lessons.content_markdown:
## A Complete Workflow

```yaml
name: Python QA Suite
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.12' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pip install pytest-html
      - run: pytest -m smoke --html=report.html --self-contained-html
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: test-report
          path: report.html
```

Running only `-m smoke` on every push (fast feedback) while a separate nightly workflow runs the full `-m regression` suite is the standard pattern for keeping CI fast without sacrificing coverage.
lessons.starter_code:
name: Python QA Suite
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: '3.12' }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -m smoke

lessons.title: Generating Reports with pytest-html and Allure
lessons.description: Turn raw pass/fail output into something stakeholders can actually read.
lessons.content_markdown:
## pytest-html

```bash
pip install pytest-html
pytest --html=report.html --self-contained-html
```
Produces a single, shareable HTML file with pass/fail breakdown, timing, and captured output per test.

## Allure (richer, industry-standard)

```bash
pip install allure-pytest
pytest --alluredir=allure-results
allure serve allure-results
```

Allure adds step-by-step breakdowns, screenshots attached inline, historical trend graphs across runs, and severity/tagging — the report format most commonly expected in professional QA teams for stakeholder-facing test results, not just pass/fail counts.
lessons.starter_code:
# pip install allure-pytest
# pytest --alluredir=allure-results
# allure serve allure-results

import allure

@allure.step("Log in as a test user")
def login(driver, email, password):
    ...

quiz_data.question: What does Allure add beyond a basic pytest-html report?
options: It runs tests faster
Step-by-step breakdowns, inline screenshots, and historical trend graphs across multiple runs
It replaces the need for assertions
It only works with Selenium, not API tests
quiz_data.explanation: Allure provides a richer, more stakeholder-friendly report format with per-step detail, attachments, and trend history — beyond a simple per-test pass/fail listing.

lessons.title: Capstone: Full API + UI Test Suite
lessons.description: Combine everything from this course into one real project.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Capstone Brief

Build a suite for a demo course platform covering:

1. **API layer**: authenticate via a fixture, test course listing/enrollment endpoints with schema validation
2. **UI layer**: Page Object Model for Login and Dashboard, verifying enrolled courses render correctly
3. **Data**: use `factory_boy` for test user generation, `responses` to mock a flaky third-party payment webhook
4. **Markers**: tag fast API tests as `smoke`, UI tests as `regression`
5. **CI**: GitHub Actions running smoke tests on every push, with an HTML report artifact

```python
class TestEnrollmentFlow:
    def test_enroll_via_api_reflects_in_dashboard(self, api_client, auth_token, driver):
        # API: enroll the user
        response = api_client.post(
            "/enrollments",
            json={"course_id": "playwright-automation"},
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {auth_token}"}
        )
        assert response.status_code == 201

        # UI: verify it shows up
        dashboard = DashboardPage(driver).load()
        assert "Playwright" in " ".join(dashboard.enrolled_course_titles())
```

This is a realistic pattern real QA engineers use daily: seed/verify state fast via the API layer, and reserve slower UI automation for confirming what a real user actually sees.

lessons.title: Capstone Knowledge Check
lessons.description: Final review covering the full course.
lessons.content_markdown:
## Final Review

Make sure you can confidently explain:

- Why virtual environments matter for avoiding "works on my machine" CI failures
- How `@pytest.mark.parametrize` reduces test-writing effort versus hand-written duplicate tests
- The difference between `function` and `session` fixture scope, and when each is correct
- Why API tests should carry more of your coverage than UI tests where possible
- When mocking an external service is the right call versus hitting it for real

If these all feel solid, you've built the full-stack QA engineering foundation this course promised — not just "Python syntax," but the actual toolkit (pytest, requests, Selenium bindings, mocking, CI) used by real automation engineers.

quiz_data.question: In the layered testing approach this course teaches, why seed/verify state via the API when possible instead of always driving the UI?
options: UI tests are being removed from the industry
API calls are faster and more reliable for setup/verification, reserving slower UI automation for what can only be confirmed visually
The API is the only thing that can be tested
UI tests cannot use fixtures
quiz_data.explanation: This is the standard 'test pyramid' reasoning: push as much verification as possible to the fast, reliable API layer, and use UI automation only for what genuinely requires rendering a real browser.
